title: DFS on Rome Streets: Deep Search Surprise ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) “dive” through Rome’s street intersections, following one path until it can’t go further—then backtracking. This reel visualizes DFS graph traversal on a real city-style network.
ig_caption: Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps ⚡ What happens when DFS commits to one road at a time? In this real-map visualization, each street intersection is a node and each intersection-to-intersection street segment is an edge. DFS explores by going deep using a stack/recursion, marking visited nodes to avoid loops, and backtracks when it hits dead-ends. Takeaway: DFS is great for exploring deep structure, but it’s not guaranteed shortest-path—use BFS for that. Debate: Should an AI navigator prefer “deep exploration” (DFS) or “shortest-first” (BFS) when routes have unknown traffic? In this Rome (Centro Storico) visualization, we build a graph from street intersections (nodes) and roads (edges), then run DFS to show how traversal dives deep, uses a stack/recursion, and backtracks when it hits dead-ends. You’ll see the exact mechanics behind dfs algorithm explained, depth first search visualised, and graph traversal (common in leetcode graph theory).
